entries.title: Germany news: Deutsche Bahn reportedly returns to profit
entries.summary: Rail operator Deutsche Bahn has reportedly returned to profit for the first time in years, helped by rising demand. Meanwhile, a court is set to make a ruling on the forwarding of private WhatsApp messages. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Deutsche Bahn reportedly returns to profit

Published July 30, 2026last updated July 30, 2026

Rail operator Deutsche Bahn has reportedly returned to profit for the first time in years, helped by rising demand. Meanwhile, a court is set to make a ruling on the forwarding of private WhatsApp messages. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany posts 0.2% quarterly growth as exports strengthen

  • Deutsche Bahn has reportedly returned to profit in its core business
  • The company made a profit in the hundreds of millions of euros in the first half of 2026

Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines to come out of Germany on Thursday, July 30:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section German economy grows by 0.2% in second quarter

German economy grows by 0.2% in second quarter

Germany's economy expanded by 0.2% in the second quarter, beating expectations for a 0.1% rise.

Preliminary figures from the federal statistics office show growth was driven mainly by stronger exports than in the previous three months.

The latest reading follows an upward revision to first-quarter growth, which is now estimated at 0.4%, up from 0.3%.

Despite the overall increase, household spending remained subdued during the quarter.

Business investment also declined from the first quarter.

The data suggest Germany's economy continued to grow through the first half of the year, supported by overseas demand despite weakness in domestic activity.

Skip next section Deutsche Bahn reportedly returns to profit in core business

Deutsche Bahn reportedly returns to profit in core business

German rail operator Deutsche Bahn has reportedly returned to profit in its core business for the first time in seven years, marking a sharp turnaround for the crisis-hit rail operator.

The state-owned company recorded a profit in the hundreds of millions of euros between January and June, the Bild newspaper and Der Spiegel news magazine reported Wednesday night.

Deutsche Bahn had posted losses of around €760 million ($870 million) in the first half of 2025.

The reports said the railway carried around 960 million passengers during the first six months of 2026, a record, and 17 million more than in the same period last year. The company was initially unavailable for comment.

Deutsche Bahn reportedly attributed much of the rise in passenger numbers to rising fuel prices. Commuters in particular switched from cars to regional trains as petrol became more expensive while rail fares remained stable.

Demand for long-distance services has also risen significantly since April.

Discount offers are also likely to have contributed to the growth. Around 600,000 people used the last-minute ticket, while 200,000 traveled with the family ticket.

Deutsche Bahn CEO Evelyn Palla is due to present the company's first-half results on Thursday.

The operator has recently faced criticism over poor punctuality, deteriorating infrastructure, and heavy financial losses. It recorded a net loss of more than EUR1 billion in 2025.

Skip next section Germany's top court weighs private WhatsApp dispute

Germany's top court weighs private WhatsApp dispute

Germany's highest civil court is considering whether forwarding private WhatsApp messages without permission can violate European data protection law.

The Federal Court of Justice (BGH) began hearing the case in Karlsruhe after two former friends became embroiled in a dispute over private WhatsApp messages concerning one woman's employer.

The messages were sent about three years ago. After the friendship broke down, one woman forwarded them to the partner of the other's boss.

The employee was subsequently dismissed and is now seeking €7,500 ($8,582) in damages from her former friend.

The BGH is considering whether the disclosure breached the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, or GDPR, and whether it infringed the claimant's personal rights.

The Frankfurt Regional Court initially awarded damages to the claimant, finding that forwarding the messages amounted to unlawful processing of personal data.

It ruled that the GDPR's "household exemption," which excludes activities that are exclusively personal or family-related, did not apply.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as Germany’s national rail operator Deutsche Bahn has reportedly returned to profit in its core business for the first time in seven years.

The beleaguered business suspects that rising fuel costs are behind the increase, with more commuters making the switch from cars to regional trains.

Meanwhile, Germany’s highest civil court is considering whether forwarding a friend’s private WhatsApp messages without permission can violate EU data protection law.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of the things that Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: India news: Assam flood toll rises to 78, more rain predicted
entries.summary: Monsoon floods in Assam have left 78 people dead so far as thousands remain displaced. Opposition lawmakers have staged a protest in the Indian parliament. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
India

India : Assam flood toll rises to 78, more rain predicted

Published July 30, 2026last updated July 30, 2026

Monsoon floods in Assam have left 78 people dead so far as thousands remain displaced. Opposition lawmakers have staged a protest in the Indian parliament. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Official figures show that flooding in Assam has claimed the lives of 78 people
  • More monsoon rain has been predicted over the next three days leading to fears of renewed flooding in vulnerable areas
  • India's opposition MPs protested in the parliament premises over the reported firing of pellet guns during the youth-led Cockroach protest movement and the donation embezzlement controversy surrounding the Ram Temple

Here are the latest developments from India on Thursday, July 30:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Opposition protest demands answers on alleged police brutality during 'Cockroach' demonstration

Opposition protest demands answers on alleged police brutality during 'Cockroach' demonstration

Parties from the INDIA bloc, the country's opposition coalition, on Thursday protested in the Parliament complex over the police action taken against the Cockroach movement youth protesters on July 20.

Opposition lawmakers were seen holding a banner with the text "Who gave the order?" as they demanded that Union Home Minister Shah answer questions in Parliament over the reported use of pellet guns on the protesters.

Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi railed against Shah for not addressing the alleged police excesses, which occurred on the first day of Parliament's second session of the year.

"Why is Amit Shah so scared of coming to Parliament and explaining the brutal violence against students?" Gandhi wrote on X.

"It reeks of guilt," the Congress leader said.

Gandhi called for the constitution of a Supreme Court-monitored high-powered committee to probe the allegations of police brutality against demonstrators.

"Students deserve justice," he said as he called for an independent committee and shared a video purportedly showing police baton-charging protesters and a man, not in uniform, throwing a protester carrying the Indian flag to the ground.

On Wednesday, Gandhi held a press conference calling for Shah's sacking as he accused the minister of ordering the police action on the youth protesters.

He alleged that Shah was either "culpable" if he gave the order or "incompetent" if he did not know what was happening as police clamped down on the protesters demanding the education minister's resignation over a major medical college entrance exam paper leak.

What has the government said on Gandhi's allegations against Amit Shah?

Union Minister Jitendra Singh on Wednesday dismissed Gandhi's claim that Shah ordered the police action.

Speaking in Parliament's lower house, the Lok Sabha, Singh questioned Gandhi's understanding of the administration, saying that orders to open fire "could only be given by a magistrate and not any minister."

Singh also said that no shots were fired at the protesters and only tear gas was used.

On Thursday, the opposition MPs also held demonstrations over an alleged donation theft linked to the Ram Temple in Ayodhya, a shrine key to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu-first politics, officials said.

Skip next section Flood-related deaths in Assam reach 78

Flood-related deaths in Assam reach 78

The number of deaths related to Assam's monsoon floods has increased to 78, the latest official tally showed Thursday.

The flooding has affected about 300,000 people across seven districts of the northeastern state. Charaideo remains the worst-hit district with 137,561 people affected by the deluge, followed by Sivasagar with 84,600 people and Jorhat with 49,911.

Heavy monsoon rains caused the 2,900-kilometer Brahmaputra River, one of Asia's largest, to burst its banks in Assam, forcing thousands into government relief camps.

The floodwaters have submerged 21,523 hectares of cropland, damaging agricultural areas across the affected districts. Nearly 17,000 livestock have been affected, while more than 11,000 animals have been washed away.

"People cannot return to their homes as their houses have either been damaged or filled with mud and silt," Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma told the media on Wednesday, adding that floodwaters have receded in many areas.

Union Home Minister Amit Shah reviewed the situation on Wednesday and assured the state of federal assistance for relief and restoration efforts, media reports said.

Meanwhile, as rescue operations continue, the India Meteorological Department has issued an alert forecasting heavy to very heavy rainfall and thunderstorms from Thursday through Saturday in isolated parts of Assam and the neighboring states of Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland.

The warning has raised concerns that vulnerable districts could face renewed flooding in the coming days.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Deaths in the devastating floods in northeastern India's Assam state have climbed to 78, as more than 300,000 people in seven districts remain affected.

Meanwhile, India's weather agency has predicted heavy to very heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms over the next two days in isolated areas across Assam.

The monsoon session of the Indian Parliament has seen another stormy day, with opposition lawmakers protesting police action during this month's 'Cockroach' youth-led demonstrations and an embezzlement controversy surrounding the Ram Temple, a flagship project of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

Stay tuned as we bring you all this and more.

entries.title: French student fined over Singapore straw licking prank
entries.summary: A social media stunt involving a single straw has left a French student facing a hefty fine — and possible consequences for his right to remain in Singapore.
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

A social media stunt involving a single straw has left a French student facing a hefty fine — and possible consequences for his right to remain in Singapore.

A French student has been fined 600 Singapore dollars (€400, $458) after licking a drinking straw and returning it to a dispenser in a prank filmed for social media.

The 19-year-old, Didier Gaspard Owen Maximilien, pleaded guilty to a public nuisance charge.

He avoided a possible prison sentence, but it remains unclear whether authorities will revoke his student pass. The French national studies at Singapore's ESSEC Business School.

What did the student do and why?

Maximilien removed a straw from a freshly squeezed orange juice vending machine in March, licked it and placed it back in the dispenser.

He filmed the stunt for an Instagram story, and the video later went viral.

An employee of the company operating the machine saw the footage and contacted police. As a result, all 500 straws in the dispenser had to be replaced.

The direct cost amounted to just 5 Singapore dollars, or around €3.30, according to court documents, but the case attracted nationwide attention.

Maximilien could have faced several months in prison, a fine, or both after being convicted of disturbing public order.

His lawyer told the court that he was remorseful and now understood that an apparently harmless prank could have far-reaching consequences.

Singapore's strict public-order laws

The wealthy city-state is known for its strict laws and rigorous enforcement, with cleanliness and tightly regulated public spaces forming part of its image for decades.

The import of chewing gum, for example, remains largely prohibited as part of efforts to prevent littering and vandalism.

Singapore also retains judicial caning for certain serious offenses, although the punishment was not applicable in the student's case.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Australia: Telegram faces legal action over failure to remove terrorist content
entries.summary: Australia says videos of terrorist executions and mass shootings weren't removed from Telegram after they were reported. The move comes a day after Russia charged founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorist activity.
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

Australia says videos of terrorist executions and mass shootings weren't removed from Telegram after they were reported. The move comes a day after Russia charged founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorist activity.

Telegram is facing a possible AU$54.6 million ($38 million, €33 million) fine in Australia as a regulator said on Thursday the messaging platform failed to remove terrorist content despite warnings.

What are the accusations against Telegram in Australia?

Australia's online safety regulator, the eSafety Commissioner, said it had begun action after videos of terrorist executions, mass shootings and other extremist material linked to attacks including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shootings and the 2022 Buffalo supermarket shooting continued to exist on Telegram.

"We allege ​that this content remained accessible on the service long after Telegram ​had been put on notice," eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant said in a statement.

The regulator said Telegram failed to remove pro-terror content between July and October 2025 or suspend the accounts responsible, despite users reporting the content and its disseminators.

"This action comes at a time when Australia is experiencing a heightened security environment against the fresh backdrop of the Bondi tragedy," Grant said, a reference to an antisemitic mass shooting at a Sydney beach that killed 15 people last year.

Telegram denied the allegations and said it would contest the case in court, adding that it had blocked thousands of extremist communities in 2026.

Russia charges Telegram founder Durov with aiding terrorism

The court action comes a day after Russia charged Telegram's billionaire founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorist activity.

Russia's Federal Security Service issued an international warrant for his arrest, alleging the platform was used by Ukrainian operatives to organize attacks inside Russia.

Soon after the news of the warrant broke, Telegram's account on X posted a picture of Durov giving a middle finger to the camera.

The Russian-born billionaire Durov, now based in Dubai, built the Telegram messaging app with his brother Nikolai and launched it in 2013. The platform currently boasts over a billion monthly active users.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Spain: Hundreds of migrants attempt to swim toward Ceuta
entries.summary: Spain's Civil Guard, maritime Rescue Services and the Red Cross said they rescued migrants from the water. The interior minister acknowledged the country was facing an "extraordinary, exceptional situation."
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

Spain's Civil Guard, maritime Rescue Services and the Red Cross said they rescued migrants from the water. The interior minister acknowledged the country was facing an "extraordinary, exceptional situation."

Spanish authorities said on Wednesday that hundreds of migrants swam from Morocco attempting to reach the territory of Ceuta.

Border security was overwhelmed by the action, as it did not expect the surge.

What do we know about the migrant attempts to reach Ceuta?

"In the last few days, more than 1,500 migrants, including adults and minors, have reached Ceuta by sea,” the leader of Ceuta's government, Juan Jesus Vivas, told journalists.

"The reception centers are collapsed and saturated," he added.

Spain's Civil Guard, maritime Rescue Services and the Red Cross reportedly rescued some 117 migrants from the water.

Moroccan authorities also reportedly grabbed dozens from the water on their way to Spanish waters.

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told Spanish television channel laSexta that authorities were facing "an extraordinary, exceptional situation."

Grande-Marlaska added that "we are dealing with it with the means that we already have deployed there permanently."

He praised Moroccan authorities for their involvement, saying they were cooperating and that the relationship with the kingdom was "close and based on loyalty."

Mostly Moroccans seeking to swim across

The Spanish government did not confirm exactly how many migrants had reached the territory by swimming.

It also remains unclear why so many people sought to swim toward Spanish territory.

The swimmers were mostly Moroccans, along with a small number of Algerians who had been living in Morocco while trying to migrate to Europe, according to activists in Morocco and Ceuta.

The incident follows a Spanish Supreme Court ruling earlier this month which established that migrants arriving by sea cannot be immediately pushed back across the border without due process, unlike those crossing by land.

However, activists have discounted the probability that average Moroccans including those swimming toward Ceuta would be aware of such a ruling, dismissing a link between the ruling and the crossings.

Migrant arrivals in Spain through the Mediterranean enclaves Ceuta and Melilla, were lower this year compared to the same time last year, as many migrants have sought other routes like the Canary Islands.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Iran war: US carries out fresh strikes in 'powerful response'
entries.summary: The US military said the strikes were in response to Iranian strikes on US forces a day earlier. Trump had threatened to hit Iran "very hard" in response to its strikes. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: US carries out new strikes in 'powerful response'

Published July 30, 2026last updated July 30, 2026

The US military said the strikes were in response to Iranian strikes on US forces a day earlier. Trump had threatened to hit Iran "very hard" in response to its strikes. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The US military has announced striking Iran in 'powerful response' to attacks a day earlier
  • Donald Trump had said the US would hit Iran 'very hard'
  • Drone hits storage tanker at Egyptian port, security firm says

Read below for the latest developments concerning the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Thursday, July 30, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Jordan shoots down five missiles launched from Iran

Jordan shoots down five missiles launched from Iran

Jordan on Thursday said its air defenses intercepted five missiles launched from Iran that were heading toward the kingdom, with no casualties reported.

"The missiles were detected, intercepted, and shot down according to established defense plans," a military statement said.

The interceptions came hours after the US military said it carried out a wave of strikes on dozens of targets in Iran.

Skip next section Two injured in US strikes, Iranian state media reports

Two injured in US strikes, Iranian state media reports

Two people were injured in the US strikes on the island of Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported on Thursday.

Meanwhile, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on late Wednesday that its forces hit dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard targets including military command centers.

The "heavy wave of strikes" were in response to Tehran's attempted missile attacks on US forces on Tuesday.

Skip next section US strikes on Iran 'completed,' military says

US strikes on Iran 'completed,' military says

The US military announced that its "heavy wave" of strikes on Iran was completed.

In a statement on X, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its latest wave of strikes hit "dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran, including military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities."

"The strikes aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf countries," US CENTCOM went on to say.

Skip next section Iranian media report attacks around Qeshm island

Iranian media report attacks around Qeshm island

Three explosions were heard on Qeshm Island in Iran near the strategic Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency.

Tasnim said that a residential area on the island was hit.

There have also been reports of explosions in Abadan and Bushehr, two cities in the southwestern part of the country.

"At 04:00 am (0030 GMT) a point near Qeshm was attacked by the American enemy military," said Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of the southern Hormozgan province, according to the Mehr news agency.

"Points around Abadan city were attacked by missiles by the terrorist enemy of America," the Fars news agency reported, citing the deputy governor of Khuzestan.

Skip next section US launches new strikes against Iran

US launches new strikes against Iran

US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that US forces began launching strikes against Iran at 8 p.m. ET (0000 GMT). 

"The strikes are a powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East," the military wrote on X.

Earlier, President Donald Trump warned that the United States would hit Iran hard in retaliation for Iranian attacks on US forces in Jordan.

Skip next section READ: Iran signals gas price hike as fuel crisis looms

READ: Iran signals gas price hike as fuel crisis looms

Iran is moving closer to politically sensitive changes in gasoline pricing as the government struggles with a widening gap between domestic fuel production and consumption, exacerbated by the ongoing conflict with the US.

On July 25, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said changes to fuel prices or rationing are "certain and unavoidable," although officials have yet to confirm whether the response will come through new quotas, higher prices or both.

Read more on how Iran, an oil powerhouse is short of gasoline.

Skip next section US-owned storage tanker hit by drone at Egyptian port — security firm

US-owned storage tanker hit by drone at Egyptian port — security firm

Ambrey, a British maritime security firm, released Wednesday an initial assessment stating that a drone had struck a US-owned gas storage tanker in the Egyptian port of Damietta.

An earlier statement from Egypt's Oil Ministry confirmed the fire at the port, but did not mention a drone attack. The ministry said the fire was dealt with immediately and there were no casualties.

It was not immediately clear who was responsible.

If confirmed, a strike by Iran or its allies would mark a significant escalation of the conflict.

US President Donald Trump said he had been briefed on the incident.

Skip next section Trump threatens to hit Iran 'very hard'

Trump threatens to hit Iran 'very hard'

US President Donald Trump said the United States would hit Iran very hard following an attack on US military personnel in Jordan.

"They’ve already apologized, but, you know, we got to smack them a little bit," he told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday.

"It’s our turn, and we’ll see if we get there with an agreement at some point. But we’re going to hit them very hard," Trump added.

The warning came after the lull in fighting appeared to end, quashing hopes of returning to negotiations.

On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia and the United States announced strikes on Iran-backed militants in Iraq, which Baghdad widely condemned. Saudi Arabia's direct involvement threatens to widen the already escalating conflict in the region.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the situation of Iran and wider Middle East.

As the conflict in the Middle East continues to escalate, US President Donald Trump vowed to retaliate against Iran for attacking US military personnel in Jordan.

Meanwhile, Ambrey, a British maritime security firm, reported that a drone strike hit a US-owned natural gas storage vessel at the Egyptian port of Damietta.

Stay tuned for more news and analysis. For our coverage of the conflict on Jul 29, 2026, you can catch our blog here.

entries.title: Explosions in Kyiv after Zelenskyy warns of Russian strikes
entries.summary: At least one person was killed in a Russian air strike on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Russia had "prepared a massive attack," citing air force reports.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Explosions in Kyiv after Zelenskyy warns of Russian strikes

July 30, 2026

At least one person was killed in a Russian air strike on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Russia had "prepared a massive attack," citing air force reports.

At least one person was killed in a Russian airstrike on Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, the city's military administration said on Thursday.

Explosions were reported over the Ukrainian capital Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia might conduct a "massive attack."

Both the Reuters and AFP news agency cited people on the ground as saying they heard explosions.

"Sadly, one death has been confirmed," the Kyiv city military administration wrote on Telegram in the early hours of Thursday.

Russia has struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles, said the city's mayor, Vitaly Klitschko, urging people to seek shelter. He added that a few non-residential sites in Kyiv caught fire.

"The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!" Klitschko said.

Several people killed in Kryvyi Rih

Russia also attacked other Ukrainian cities overnight. At least six people, including two girls, were killed in a Russian missile strike on the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, according to the head of the local military administration.

"In a village on the outskirts of Kryvyi Rih, a direct strike by an Iskander-M ballistic missile, launched from Voronezh, hit a private house where a large family lived, killing girls aged five and 12 and four adults," Oleksandr Vilkul said.

He added that a further eight people were wounded and that the death toll may rise.

Russian missiles also damaged two apartment buildings and injured six people in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine close to the Polish border, according to local officials.

Meanwhile, the Polish Armed Forces announced on X that Poland had scrambled its fighter jets on Thursday to protect its airspace amid Russian air strikes on Ukraine.

"Fighter aircraft and an early warning aircraft have begun operations while ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness," the post said, adding that the actions are of a preventive nature.

What did Zelenskyy say ahead of the Kyiv explosions?

The strikes come as Zelenskyy had warned of a "high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight."

"I received a report from Air Force Commander Anatolii Kryvonozhko. The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago," Zelenskyy said on X.

The Ukrainian president stressed that Ukrainians' safety depended on the willingness of Kyiv's allies to provide anti-missile defenses. His statements came on the heels of a trip to the US where he said President Donald Trump had agreed to give Ukraine licenses for Patriot missiles.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Report finds 2025 was deadliest year for antisemitic attacks outside Israel
entries.summary: Germany had the highest number of antisemitic incidents in 2025, both in absolute and relative terms, a report has found.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

Germany had the highest number of antisemitic incidents in 2025, both in absolute and relative terms, a report has found.

A report released on Wednesday by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism group found a record rise in antisemitic attacks worldwide.

J7 looked at Jewish communities in Argentina, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Britain and the United States, which together are home to more than 90% of Jewish people outside of Israel.

The report highlighted that some 20 people were murdered in antisemitic attacks in Australia, the UK and the US in 2025, in what was "the deadliest year for antisemitic attacks in the diaspora... since the AMIA attack in Buenos Aires in 1994," the report said.

The AMIA attack was a bombing that targeted a Jewish community center, leaving 85 people killed.

The deadliest event in 2025 was the mass shooting at a Hanukkah festival near Australia's Bondi Beach, where 15 people were killed.

"Antisemitism in our seven countries is no longer a surge; it is our new normal," the J7 task force said in a statement.

"Governments must stop reacting after Jews are attacked and start acting before, with real security funding, stronger laws and social media platforms that enforce their own rules," the statement said.

J7's report found more than 23,000 antisemitic incidents across the seven countries in 2025, a sharp rise from the 9,800 that were recorded in 2022.

Gaza war remains a factor

The report highlighted that anti-Zionism appeared to be a key motivating factor for the rise in antisemitism, accounting for 48% of incidents in Britain and 45% in the US.

According to the report, incidents increased in the years after the Gaza war, which was triggered after Hamas's deadly October 7 attack in 2023.

The report found a rise of 136% in antisemitic incidents from 2022 to 2025.

Although the total number of incidents fell from 2024 to 2025, the figure remains well above pre-October 7, 2023, levels, the report said.

Germany tops list of antisemitic attacks

While Australia topped the seven countries in terms of the sharp rise in antisemitic incidents, Germany stood out as the one with the highest number of antisemitic incidents, both in absolute and relative terms, the report found, nearly five times Australia's rate.



In 2025, there were nearly 70 incidents per 1,000 Jewish residents, with a total number of 8,725 cases up from 8,713 in 2024 and 2,610 in 2022

Right-wing extremism caused 807 of the total cases, up from 562 in 2024.

Meanwhile, the number of antisemitic attacks attributed to left-wing, anti-imperialist extremism also rose from 349 to 501 cases. Islamist extremist-linked incidents rose from 143 to 166.

The report found that "anti-Israel activism" accounted for 22.6% of all recorded incidents in Germany in 2025.

Josef Schuster, president of the German Central Council of Jews in Germany, said the numbers represented an "ongoing normalization of antisemitism" in Germany.

Schuster called on lawmakers "to close existing loopholes in criminal law and consistently criminalize calls for the destruction of the State of Israel."

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: How well are LGBTQ+ rights protected across Europe?
entries.summary: After the attack on Berlin’s Pride event on Saturday, the situation of the LGBTQ+ community in Germany is a topic of conversation. How well are queer rights protected in other European countries? An overview.
entries.content:
Europe

How well are LGBTQ+ rights protected across Europe?

July 29, 2026

After the attack on Berlin’s Pride event on Saturday, the situation of the LGBTQ+ community in Germany is a topic of conversation. How well are queer rights protected in other European countries? An overview.

Germany is still reeling from the weekend's car attack on its Berlin Pride celebration. Politicians are deep in discussion over which consequences the country should draw.

The center-left Social Democrats (SPD) are now mounting another effort to have LGBTQ+ rights enshrined in the German constitution, known as the Basic Law. Article 3 of the Basic Law addresses equality before the law, and currently states that, "no person shall be favored or disfavored because of sex, parentage, race, language, homeland and origin, faith or religious or political opinions. No person shall be disfavored because of disability." 

But no mention is made of gender identity or sexual orientation. The SPD wants to change that.

Germany: progressive, but with gaps

Germany still has areas in which queer people — that is, individuals who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, intersex, asexual, non-binary, pangender and otherwise — are not yet fully equal under the law. In addition to the lack of constitutional protection, parentage law is a concern as well.

When a heterosexual couple has a child, the biological mother and her husband are automatically recognized as the child's legal parents. (When a heterosexual couple is unmarried, the biological father must submit a formal declaration to the youth welfare office to recognize his paternity to legally be considered the child's father.)

In queer family constellations, however, the legal situation is far more complex and often requires lengthy legal proceedings to establish parentage. Surrogacy, meanwhile, is illegal in German — a position the ruling conservative Christian Democratic (CDU) party has held for years. Despite having defended this position in the past, high-ranking CDU politician Jens Spahn recently disclosed he had sidestepped this ban and that he and his husband received a child via surrogacy in the US. He was pressured to resign from his position as parliamentary group leader as a result.

Hate crimes and violent attacks on queer people have increased, and many continue to report discrimination in their daily lives. But compared with other European nations, Germany still ranks relatively highly in terms of legal equality for queer people.

In a cross-comparison of 49 European countries, the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association (ILGA), a global umbrella organization for LGBTQ+ advocacy groups, ranks Germany seventh in terms of protection and equality for queer residents. Spain holds first place, while Russia comes in last place. 

Spain: a pioneer in Europe

Spain's pioneering role in LGBTQ+ rights is rooted in its recent history. Before the end of Francisco Franco's dictatorship in 1975, queer people in Spain were persecuted and imprisoned. The transformation that followed brought about a wave of liberalization and modernization.

The process of decriminalizing homosexuality began in 1979. In 2005, Spain opened marriage to same-sex couples, including full adoption rights. In 2023, the Spanish parliament passed a comprehensive self-determination law. Any person aged 16 or older can now change their legal gender and first name in official documents with a simple declaration at the civil registry office.

Transgender identities are no longer classified as disorders in Spain's healthcare system. Spain also has strong anti-discrimination laws, an independent equality authority, and a legal requirement for companies with more than 50 employees to implement active inclusion and diversity plans for LGBTQ+ staff.

According to regular surveys, these legal advances enjoy the support of a broad majority of Spain's population. Pride events such as Madrid Pride are among the largest in the world and receive support from government institutions across the political spectrum.

Other European countries with similarly progressive records include Malta, Iceland, Belgium and Denmark.

Italy: growing restrictions amid a shift to the right

Under the right-wing nationalist government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, pressure on the LGBTQ+ community has grown significantly in recent years.

Italy still does not have marriage equality, nor does it grant adoption rights to queer couples. The Interior Ministry and public prosecutors have even challenged previously issued birth certificates, resulting in some non-biological mothers being stripped of their legal motherhood years after their children were born.

In late 2024, Italy's parliament passed a law declaring surrogacy a "universal crime." As a result, citizens who have children through surrogacy abroad may face prison sentences and substantial fines upon their return.

Italy also lacks a national anti-discrimination law that explicitly criminalizes hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Arcigay, the country's largest LGBTQ+ organization, has recorded a worrying increase in violent offenses and hate crimes targeting queer people.

Hungary: Orban's legacy and its reversal?

Hungary's legal environment for LGBTQ+ people is also restrictive and has been shaped by years of systematic legislative tightening under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

In 2020, Hungary abolished the possibility for transgender people to amend the sex recorded in their birth register. Hungary's constitution explicitly defines marriage as a "union of one man and one woman." Same-sex couples are barred from adoption. In 2021, Hungary passed a law under the guise of "child protection" that prohibits any positive portrayal of homosexuality or transgender identities to minors. The law has since been ruled incompatible with EU law by the European Court of Justice.

However, Orban's successor, Peter Magyar, who took office in May 2026, may now be steering the country in a different direction. One indication for this was Budapest Pride in June 2026, which was a peaceful celebration attended by tens of thousands.

The event had been banned the year prior, with the government at the time citing assembly laws.

Magyar's government has also announced plans to fundamentally revise existing anti-LGBTQ+ legislation and bring it into line with EU law. But the queer community in Hungary remains cautious. Repealing Orban-era legislation is likely to be a complex undertaking that could face stiff political and social resistance.

Russia: systematic persecution

Russia has the most repressive anti-LGBTQ+ legislation in Europe according to the ILGA Rainbow Map. The Russian Supreme Court has designated what it called the "LGBT movement" as "extremist" and banned it — even though no such organization exists. Authorities continue carrying out raids targeting activists, publishers and private individuals. Prison sentences can go up to 12 years. Positive or neutral expressions of LGBTQ+ identities and lives is criminalized, and gender recognition procedures are banned. 

The Russian LGBTQ+ community has been under particular pressure since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which President Vladimir Putin has in the past argued is a proxy battle with the West and its attempts to undermine the "traditional family values" of Russian society by promoting LGBTQ+ rights.

Under the extremist designation, queer people in Russia, as well as relatives and supporting activists, often live in fear of police and state violence. Many have fled the country.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: France expels Russian media commentator over disinformation
entries.summary: Tensions between Xenia Fedorova and the French date back to 2017, when President Emmanuel Macron accused her of spreading "defamatory falsehoods."
entries.content:
France

France expels Russian media commentator over disinformation

July 29, 2026

Tensions between Xenia Fedorova and the French date back to 2017, when President Emmanuel Macron accused her of spreading "defamatory falsehoods."

Russian commentator Xenia Fedorova has been ordered to leave France, the country's Interior Ministry said Wednesday. She has been accused of disseminating Kremlin propaganda on French television and radio.

According to French newspaper Liberation, the expulsion order accuses Fedorova of acting "as a conduit for disinformation campaigns orchestrated by the Russian authorities" with the aim of "destabilising public order" in France.

According to the AFP news agency, Fedorova has been placed under house arrest since the order was issued.

Fedorova is the former chief of the Russia Today (RT) in France, which was ultimately banned in the country after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

She stayed in the country and became a commentator for broadcasting outlets owned by French billionaire Vincent Bollore's media conglomerate.

According to French daily Le Monde, Fedorova has been known to be a "protege" of Bollore.

Fedorova made frequent appearances on the CNews television channel and Europe 1 radio.

She also writes for Le Journal du Dimanche newspaper, where she has been accused of spreading Kremlin talking points about Ukraine and the West.

'Serious infringement' on free speech

Fedorova's employers reacted to her expulsion saying they were astonished, adding that the move amounted to "a particularly serious infringement of freedom of expression."

The media group said it would "provide their full support ‌to Ms. Fedorova during this decision."

The commentator's lawyer Emmanuel Piwnica told AFP that his client would "immediately" file an appeal against the order.

"Xenia Fedorova is a journalist," Piwnica told AFP, adding that she has "always carried out her work in the most proper manner possible."

Macron says Fedorova 'not a journalist'

Tensions between Fedorova and the French state go back as far as 2017, when President Emmanuel Macron criticized her and implied she was not a journalist.

"When media outlets spread defamatory falsehoods, they are no longer journalists. They are instruments of influence," Macron said.

In June, Macron was again asked to speak on the subject and he said his opinion had not changed.

Experts on disinformation had previously raised the alarm about the influence of figures like Fedorova in France, ahead of a presidential election next year.

Although there is no evidence of any links between Fedorova and the Kremlin, media advocates have said she should still be regarded as an agent of influence.

Edited by: Sean Sinico
